overview.statement: By 2002 everyone in Thailand was covered by one of three public schemes: the Civil Servant Medical Benefit Scheme (CSMBS) for civil servants and their dependants, Social Health Insurance (SHI) for private-sector employees, and the Universal Coverage Scheme (UCS) for the rest of the population.

The UCS rests on the National Health Security Act 2002 and is run by an autonomous public agency; SHI rests on the Social Security Act 1990 and is run by a department of the Ministry of Labour; the CSMBS rests on a 1980 Royal Decree, amended in 2010, and is run by a bureau of the Ministry of Finance's Comptroller-General's Department.
The 2024 review puts population coverage at 7% for the CSMBS, 18% for SHI and 71% for the UCS; private health insurance is an extra layer for people able to pay premiums.
Creating the National Health Security Office (NHSO) changed the Ministry of Public Health from both buyer and provider of care into mainly a provider, with the NHSO buying care for UCS members.
Care is delivered mostly by the public sector: in 2021 Ministry of Public Health facilities held 67.2% of hospital beds and private hospitals 19.5%.

financing.statement: The UCS and the CSMBS are paid for from general taxation; SHI is paid for by contributions shared equally by employers, employees and the government; private health insurance is paid for by premiums from individuals or households.

The SHI contribution is not only for health: it also pays for maternity benefits, disability and death benefits, cash allowances and old-age pensions, and it is compulsory for private-sector employees.

locator.section: 3.3 Population coverage and basis for entitlement

financing.statement: According to the 2024 review, the SHI contribution was 5% of salary, assessed on pay up to THB 15,000 a month; that ceiling had not been raised since SHI began in 1991, while the minimum wage was adjusted every year.

Because of the contribution ceiling, the 2024 review found almost no difference between what minimum-wage workers and white-collar employees earning THB 80,000-100,000 a month paid into SHI, and it called the ceiling a source of regressivity.
Most of Thailand's tax revenue comes from indirect taxes, chiefly value added tax, followed by direct taxes such as personal and corporate income tax; this mix was unchanged between 1995 and 2019.
Personal income tax, the largest direct tax, is progressive: rates run from 0% on annual income under THB 150,000 to 35% on income over THB 5 million.

People fund the public schemes through personal income tax, corporate tax paid by employers, indirect taxes such as the 7% value added tax, and, for private-sector employees and their employers, SHI contributions.

A 2% surcharge on top of tobacco and alcohol excise tax is earmarked by law for the Thai Health Promotion Foundation (ThaiHealth), an autonomous public agency that runs campaigns on major health risks.

In national health accounts for 2019, general government funding paid for 63.2% of current health spending, Social Health Insurance 9.0%, voluntary private insurance 13.6%, compulsory road-traffic insurance 3.0%, out-of-pocket payments 8.5% and employer benefits 1.9%.

Using the WHO definition of domestic general government health expenditure, which counts social insurance as government spending, public funding rose from 43.1% of current health expenditure in 1995 to 72.2% in 2019, while private domestic funding fell from 56.9% to 27.7%.

locator.section: 7 Assessment of health systems, chapter summary

financing.statement: UCS and SHI money is pooled centrally under closed-ended budgets, whereas the CSMBS has an open-ended budget and so is not pooled for risk-sharing.
Personal income tax relief applies to premiums for voluntary health insurance (and life insurance), which can be deducted as an annual expense as an incentive to buy cover.

For tax year 2020, a taxpayer could deduct own health insurance premiums paid to an insurer operating in Thailand up to THB 25,000, within a combined THB 100,000 limit together with life insurance premiums and certain bank deposits.

For tax year 2020, premiums paid for the health insurance of the taxpayer's or spouse's parents could be deducted up to THB 15,000 in total, provided each parent's own assessable income did not exceed THB 30,000.
By 2022, prevention and health promotion managed by the NHSO had risen to 12% of the UCS capitation budget formula.

covered.statement: The CSMBS is a tax-financed scheme with no contributions that covers government employees, pensioners and their dependants (parents, spouse and up to three children under 20).

locator.section: 3.3 Population coverage and basis for entitlement

covered.statement: SHI covers the worker only, not family members, except that its maternity benefit extends to the spouse of a male member.

locator.section: 3.3 Population coverage and basis for entitlement

covered.statement: The UCS adds new interventions to its package only after assessment against a cost-effectiveness threshold of THB 160,000 per quality-adjusted life year, long-term affordability and the system's capacity to deliver; when the National Health Security Board adopts one, it also approves the budget for it, so no new benefit goes unfunded.

locator.section: 6.1.2 Extension of the UCS benefit package

covered.statement: The National List of Essential Medicines is the drug benefit list for all three public schemes, and the CSMBS and SHI generally take up new benefits adopted by the UCS.

locator.section: 6.1.2 Extension of the UCS benefit package

covered.statement: In 2021 the UCS added liver transplantation for intermediate and late-stage cirrhosis and ECMO for acute heart or lung failure to its benefit package.

Benefits added to the UCS package in 2022-2023 include dental implants for members without teeth, thalassaemia screening for pregnant women and their partners, hepatitis B and C screening for people born before 1992, newborn screening for congenital heart disease by pulse oximetry, and HIV self-testing.
Prevention and health-promotion services financed by the NHSO cover the whole population, not only UCS members; for example, HPV vaccination for girls aged 11-12 through schools was added in 2017.
Mammography screening had not been added to the UCS benefit package at the time of the 2024 review.

High-cost medicines that do not offer good value for money are excluded from public reimbursement in Thailand; the authors, from the government's HTA agency, propose a separate pathway for some life-saving high-cost medicines that fail the cost-effectiveness threshold.

cost_sharing.statement: Care from contracted providers is free for UCS members, with no deductibles, no coverage ceiling and no extra billing by providers.

UCS members paid a flat THB 30 per visit or admission from 2002 until the charge was abolished in November 2008; it was brought back in 2012 with 21 exempt groups, including people who do not wish to pay it.

Point-of-service charges differ by scheme: the CSMBS allows balance billing for anything above its maximum reimbursement rate, SHI allows capped extra billing for some items such as private rooms and dental care, and the UCS charges THB 30 per visit or admission.

SHI members mostly pay nothing out of pocket, but some services carry reimbursement ceilings: dental care is reimbursed up to THB 900 a year, and in 2021 maternity care was a THB 1,500 antenatal allowance plus a THB 15,000 lump sum per pregnancy, with members paying anything above these amounts.
Out-of-pocket payments fell from 44.9% of current health spending in 1995 to 8.5% in 2019 (national health accounts).

Analysing national surveys from 2019 and 2021, a study found that the type of public insurance a person had was linked to out-of-pocket medical and transport spending only to a small degree, but people with high needs, such as chronic conditions, bore heavier out-of-pocket medical and transport costs.

financial_hardship.statement: In a nationwide study of 1,224 patients with chronic kidney disease (interviews June 2019 to January 2021), catastrophic health expenditure, defined as spending at least 40% of household capacity to pay, affected 50.0% of UCS haemodialysis patients and 19.5% of UCS peritoneal dialysis patients under the 'PD First' policy then in place; in the poorest UCS quintile all haemodialysis patients and two-thirds of peritoneal dialysis patients were medically impoverished, and travel costs were the main driver for haemodialysis.

Clinicians at a public neurological institute in Bangkok write that the UCS does not reimburse travel, caregivers' accommodation or food, and that these unpaid costs weigh most on rural patients who must travel far for care.

additional_care.statement: Private health insurance is voluntary; insurers commonly screen applicants and exclude existing conditions, usually refuse people over 60, and renew or end policies each year with premiums reset according to the previous year's use and claims.

There is no complementary private insurance, because the public benefit packages are comprehensive; private policies offer benefits similar to the public schemes but with a wider choice of private hospitals.
Voluntary private health insurance grew from 2.5% of current health spending in 1995 to 13.6% in 2019 (national health accounts).
Large private hospitals in Bangkok, including chains listed on the stock market, mostly serve international patients.

access.statement: Thailand had 4.10 doctors, nurses and midwives per 1,000 people in 2020, below the WHO indicative benchmark of 4.45 per 1,000 set in 2016.
In the 2021 public health resources survey, Bangkok had 19.2 doctors per 10,000 people against 3.6 in the North-east and 5.9 nationwide; the survey counts only professionals who responded.
Unmet need for care was low in 2019: 1.4% for outpatient care, 1.1% for dental care and about 0.1% for inpatient care; the main reasons given were cost, difficulty reaching services and long waits.

locator.section: 7.3.3 Equity of access to health care

access.statement: No published data exist on average waiting times in Ministry of Public Health hospitals; one study found that over a quarter of colorectal cancer patients waited more than a month to start treatment, against a ministry goal of operating within four weeks of staging.
Outpatient visits per UCS member rose from 2.45 a year in 2003 to 3.45 in 2020, and admissions from 0.09 to 0.12 per member per year, with both trends levelling off in recent years.

Between 2015 and 2024 the number of general practitioners and specialists grew, and the geographic inequality of GPs fell sharply (Gini coefficient 0.42 in 2015, 0.22 in 2024), which the authors attribute to mandatory service and rural recruitment.

Specialists in established, scarce fields such as gynaecology, anaesthesiology and neurosurgery became more concentrated between regions over 2015-2024, clustering in central provinces and around Bangkok.

outcomes.statement: The GBD study put Thailand's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index at 62.5 (95% uncertainty interval 58.2-66.5) for ages 0-74 in 2019.
Maternal mortality fell from 48 per 100,000 live births in 2000 to 29 in 2020.

locator.section: 7 Assessment of health systems, chapter summary

outcomes.statement: Effective coverage of diabetes (HbA1c-based control) rose from 8.1% in 2016 to 11.7% in 2019 and of hypertension from 11.3% to 15.7%, which the review calls still relatively low.
An analysis of national databases found that only 5-8% of women in the target ages of 30-59 were screened for cervical cancer in 2020-2022.

Using 2016-2020 UCS inpatient claims, a 2023 study estimated that about 7% of hospitalised UCS patients suffered medical harm, costing about THB 9.6 billion a year, around 5.5% of the 2021 UCS budget.

Among provincial hospitals under the Ministry of Public Health, hospital networks whose provincial hospital was accredited had lower standardised mortality ratios for acute stroke and sepsis, in a 5-year analysis of UCS claims.

locator.section: 7.4.2 Health service outcomes and quality of care

outcomes.statement: Noncommunicable diseases accounted for 8 of the 10 leading causes of death and 7 of the 10 leading causes of lost disability-adjusted life years in 2019.
Adult smoking fell from 23% in 2004 to 17.4% in 2021, helped by measures including higher tobacco tax, but the decline is projected to fall short of a 30% reduction by 2025.

costs.statement: The approved UCS budget per member rose from US$29 in 2003 to US$115 in 2020, with annual growth slowing from 8.1% in 2005 to 4.9% in 2020.

In 2019, government spending on health per CSMBS member was about six times that per UCS member; CSMBS costs climbed fast after direct billing of the government for outpatient care was fully applied in 2008.
Thailand borrowed THB 1 trillion for its COVID-19 response; 70.9% went to mitigating the impact on people and businesses, 22.7% to economic and social recovery and 6.4% to the health sector response.
A review of the medicines system under UHC found steadily rising drug spending, driven by very expensive technologies, and growing reliance on imported finished medicines.

what_works.statement: The UCS subsidy is pro-poor: in 2021 the poorest wealth quintile made up 23.5% of UCS members but received 28.4% of the public subsidy for outpatient care and 21.6% for inpatient care, while the richest quintile (14.4% of members) received 11.2% and 14.7%.

locator.section: 7.3.3 Equity of access to health care

what_works.statement: Using national household surveys, the share of households spending more than 10% of consumption on health fell from 6.0% in 1996 to 1.9% in 2020, and the share pushed below the poverty line by health payments from 2.2% to 0.2%.

Paying providers mainly by capitation and diagnosis-related groups within fixed budgets (SHI since 1991, UCS since 2002) brought large efficiency gains, encouraging cheaper generic medicines and rational prescribing.

To staff rural services, Thailand combined recruiting students from rural backgrounds, rural-focused curricula, compulsory rural service for all new doctors, nurses, pharmacists and dentists since 1972, incentives, and task-shifting to nurse practitioners and other cadres.

locator.section: 4 Physical and human resources, chapter summary

what_works.statement: Compared with other upper-middle-income countries, Thailand had lower child mortality and longer life expectancy for its health spending per person (latest year 2020), which the review suggests may reflect its closed-ended provider payment.

During the COVID-19 pandemic a full package of tests, treatment, isolation and vaccination was free to everyone in Thailand, Thai or not, and public and private providers were paid the same rates for it.
The Health Intervention and Technology Assessment Program (HITAP), set up in 2007, built health technology assessment capacity in Thailand and linked research to policy and practice.

problems.statement: Because the three schemes were created at different times with different provider payment methods, the system remains fragmented and the services members receive can differ between schemes.
Access to higher-cost drugs is unequal across the three schemes: the closed-ended UCS and SHI give access to more cost-effective but narrower drug choices than the fee-for-service CSMBS.

Many health workers are leaving: nurses and newly qualified doctors resign at high rates because of heavy workloads and low pay, and the push to make Thailand a medical hub has drawn staff from rural to urban areas and from public to private hospitals.

locator.section: 4 Physical and human resources, chapter summary

problems.statement: The number of general practitioners in the public sector began to decline after 2019 despite overall growth, while private-sector specialist numbers grew faster than GPs.
Low-skilled migrant workers in the informal sector rely on the Ministry of Public Health's Health Insurance Card Scheme, which is semi-voluntary, with no legal mechanism making migrants enrol.

A scoping review reports that only about a third of migrants in Thailand had enrolled in migrant health insurance, and that migrants face barriers such as lacking legal documents and money, language and lack of information.

Devolving health centres to local government has been slow: in 2021 only 84 of 9,759 Ministry of Public Health health centres (0.8%) had been devolved, as subdistrict administrations lacked readiness, capacity and funding.

reforms.statement: As of October 2025 the Public Health Minister was driving a '30-Baht Treatment Anywhere, Free Dialysis Everywhere' initiative, with plans for kidney transplant services in all 12 health regions; the NHSO was revising its reimbursement guidelines so that patients can choose, with medical advice, the type of dialysis that suits them.

The '30-baht Treatment Anywhere' programme, piloted in four provinces from 7 January 2024, was extended to all provinces from 1 January 2025; it lets UCS members be treated outside their assigned hospital, within the same province, by showing their ID card.
In 2022 the UCS dropped the rule that patients choosing haemodialysis had to pay for it themselves, widening their choice of kidney replacement therapy.

From 2021, UCS members diagnosed with cancer may be treated at any hospital, and may use any primary care provider for outpatient care for reasons they define, without the referral from their registered network previously required.

The review found no major health reform between 2015 and 2024 other than devolving subdistrict health centres from the Ministry of Public Health to Provincial Administrative Organizations, launched on a large scale in 2022, with no published evidence yet on its effects.
The Primary Health Care System Act of 2019 promotes family doctor care teams; the review notes its effects still need to be assessed.

us_lessons.statement: Analysing Thailand's reform as a lesson for other countries, the authors conclude that the reform team's ability to generate and use evidence kept the reform on track despite opposition and path dependence.

The same study names two contested changes as key to securing enough money for and good governance of the UCS: a budgeting process that curbed the Bureau of Budget's discretion, and the split between the purchaser (NHSO) and the main provider (Ministry of Public Health).
HITAP's own staff report that its semi-autonomous structure helped it build health technology assessment and suggest its experience may be relevant to other countries setting up HTA programmes.

Reviewing countries with established HTA systems, including Australia, England and South Korea, a study found nearly all had set up special programmes to pay for high-cost medicines that are not cost-effective, and recommended that Thailand not reimburse cost-ineffective medicines except where they are the only life-saving option.
Authors of a national workforce study present Thailand's evidence-based, equity-focused workforce policies as lessons for other low- and middle-income countries pursuing universal coverage.
